title: Nutra compliance
summary: Health claims law, platform health policies, the bans on before-and-after images and fake experts, honest testimonials and a pre-launch review you run every time. In nutra the words decide whether you keep your account, your payouts and your buyers' trust.

lessons.title: Why compliance is the business: the claims ladder
objectives: By the end you can sort any health statement into disease, function, cosmetic or general claims.
By the end you can rewrite a disease claim into an honest claim the product can support.
By the end you can work out what a ban really costs compared with honest ads.

steps.p: In nutra, one wrong sentence can get an ad rejected, an ad account disabled, a payment frozen or a regulator involved. Worse, it can push a sick person to skip real treatment. Honest claims are the only way to build something that lasts longer than a few weeks.
steps.say: In nutra, compliance isn't paperwork. One wrong sentence can get an ad rejected, an ad account disabled, a payment frozen, or a regulator involved. Worse, it can push a sick person to skip real treatment. So remember this: the words are the risk, and the words are yours. Honest claims are the only way to build something that lasts longer than a few weeks.

steps.p: Example: an operator earns $150 profit a day on one ad account. A cure claim gets it disabled. Rebuilding with new, compliant creatives and a properly verified account takes three weeks, if an appeal or new account is allowed at all.
steps.more: Example only. $150 × 21 = $3,150 of lost profit, plus the cost of new creatives and any money stuck on the old account. Some platforms do not allow you to open new accounts after a disable, and trying to get around that breaks their rules. The cheap shortcut is very expensive.

d.label: profit lost in 3 weeks
d.note: Example: $150 × 21 days, before creative and setup costs.

steps.say: Here's what one ban can cost, as an example. An operator earns one hundred and fifty dollars profit a day on one ad account. A cure claim gets it disabled. Rebuilding with new, compliant creatives and a properly verified account takes three weeks, if an appeal or new account is allowed at all. One fifty times twenty one days is three thousand one hundred and fifty dollars of lost profit, before creative and setup costs. And some platforms don't allow new accounts after a disable, and trying to get around that breaks their rules. The cheap shortcut is very expensive.

steps.p: Health statements fall into rough steps. The higher the step, the more proof and permission it needs. Disease claims are for licensed medicines only. Your ads should live on the lower steps, and only with evidence from the advertiser.
steps.more: Exact rules differ by country. In the EU and UK, health claims on foods and supplements must come from an approved list. In the US, supplements may make structure or function claims with evidence and a set disclaimer, but not disease claims. Lesson 2 covers the regions.

rows: Only with evidence and where law allows

steps.say: Health statements fall into rough steps, called the claims ladder. The higher the step, the more proof and permission it needs. At the top, disease claims, like cures arthritis, are for licensed medicines only. Function claims, like supports joint comfort, need evidence and only where the law allows. Cosmetic claims, like moisturises dry skin, are fine if true. Product facts, like contains menthol and arnica, fine if true. And experience, like a cooling feel, fine if typical. Exact rules differ by country, and Lesson two covers the regions.

steps.p: Most disease claims can be rewritten into something honest about what the product is and does. The honest version is less dramatic, but it survives review, brings buyers who are not disappointed at the door and keeps you on the right side of the law.

b.title: Honest version
items: A cooling cream for tired joints
What is in the cream and why
A routine to support healthy habits

steps.say: Most disease claims can be rewritten into something honest. On the left, illegal or banned: cures arthritis in seven days, reverses diabetes, doctors hate this, lose ten kilos in a week. On the right, the honest versions: a cooling cream for tired joints, a low sugar meal plan guide, what's in the cream and why, a routine to support healthy habits. Less dramatic, yes. But it survives review, brings buyers who aren't disappointed at the door, and keeps you on the right side of the law.

steps.p: Example: paste your ad copy into a document and mark each sentence with its step on the ladder. Anything marked disease claim, or with no evidence in your claims file, is rewritten before launch.
steps.say: Here's how to check copy line by line. In this example, each sentence of the ad is marked with its step on the ladder. Ends arthritis pain fast is a disease claim, so no. Cooling menthol cream is a product fact, so yes. Loved by ten thousand Nigerians is unverified, so only if proven. Pay on delivery is a fact, so yes. Anything marked disease claim, or with no evidence in your claims file, is rewritten before launch.

steps.p: Run every sentence in your ad and lander through these questions. If one answer is no, change the sentence. Ask the advertiser for the evidence in writing, and keep it in a claims file for each offer.
d: Is it allowed in this country?
Is it allowed on this platform?
Would a typical buyer get this?
steps.say: Run every sentence in your ad and lander through these questions, in order. Is it about a disease? Can the advertiser prove it? Is it allowed in this country? Is it allowed on this platform? And would a typical buyer get this result? If one answer is the wrong way, change the sentence. Ask the advertiser for the evidence in writing, and keep it in a claims file for each offer.

steps.h: Words that signal a disease claim
steps.p: These words almost always turn a sentence into a medical claim. If you see them in your copy, rewrite. Networks sometimes put them in the provided landers; that does not make them legal for you to use.
steps.say: These words almost always turn a sentence into a medical claim. Cure, heal and treat are medicine words. Prevent is a disease prevention claim. Disease names, like diabetes, arthritis and hypertension. Replace medication, which is dangerous and illegal. Guaranteed results, misleading by nature. And miracle, secret or banned, which is misleading hype. If you see them in your copy, rewrite. Networks sometimes put them in the landers they provide, and that doesn't make them legal for you to use.

steps.h: The network's lander is your risk too
steps.p: Many offers come with landers full of disease claims and invented doctors. If you send traffic there, platforms and regulators can treat the claims as yours. Check every page you link to, and use your own honest lander if the provided one fails.

d.text: You are responsible for every claim your ad sends people to, including the network's lander. Teach and use honest claims only.

steps.say: Here's a warning. Many offers come with landers full of disease claims and invented doctors. If you send traffic there, platforms and regulators can treat those claims as yours. So check every page you link to, and use your own honest lander if the provided one fails. You're responsible for every claim your ad sends people to, including the network's lander.

steps.p: Example: an ad for a joint cream that stays on the lower steps of the ladder. It names the feel, the ingredients and the payment method, and it says plainly what the product is not. This is the kind of copy this school teaches.

page.h: A cooling cream for tired knees
page.p: Menthol and arnica in a light cream. Many users like the cool feel after a long day. Not a medicine. If pain persists, see a doctor. Pay on delivery.

steps.say: Here's an example of an honest ad for a joint cream that stays on the lower steps of the ladder. The headline: a cooling cream for tired knees. It names the ingredients, menthol and arnica, and the feel, a cool feel after a long day. Then it says plainly, not a medicine, and if pain persists, see a doctor. And the payment method, pay on delivery. This is the kind of copy this school teaches.

steps.h: Honest ads can win on value
steps.p: Example: two ads for the same cream, 100 leads each. The exaggerated one gets cheaper leads but poor approval and buyout, because buyers feel misled on the call or at the door. Compare profit per 100 leads, not cost per lead.
steps.more: Example. Exaggerated ad: CPL $4, so 100 leads cost $400. Approval 30% gives 30 approved. Buyout falls under the offer's line, so the network cuts the payout to $14: 30 × $14 = $420, profit $20, if the ad is not rejected first. Honest ad: CPL $5, 100 leads cost $500. Approval 50% gives 50 approved × $20 = $1,000, profit $500.
steps.say: Here's an example of two ads for the same cream, a hundred leads each. The exaggerated one gets cheaper leads, four dollars each, but only thirty percent approval, and buyout falls so the payout is cut to fourteen dollars. Profit, twenty dollars, if it isn't rejected first. The honest ad costs five dollars a lead, but fifty percent approve at twenty dollars, so profit is five hundred dollars. Look at the gap between those bars. Compare profit per hundred leads, not cost per lead.

steps.p: These are the claim mistakes that cause most nutra bans. Each has a simple fix that only costs you a little drama in the copy.
steps.more: 'May cure arthritis' is still a cure claim. Softening words do not change the meaning a buyer takes away. Regulators judge the overall impression an ad gives, not the exact wording.
steps.say: These claim mistakes cause most nutra bans. On the left: copying a rival's claims, using the network lander unchecked, adding may to a cure claim, and having no claims file. On the right, the fixes: write from the evidence, audit or replace the lander, rewrite to a true claim, and keep evidence per offer. And about that may: may cure arthritis is still a cure claim. Regulators judge the overall impression an ad gives, not the exact wording.

steps.p: Keep one simple folder per offer. If a platform, network or regulator asks why you said something, you can show it. It also stops you from drifting into stronger claims as you make new creatives.
d: Evidence for each claim, in writing
steps.say: Keep one simple folder per offer, your claims file. It holds the product registration details, the ingredient list from the advertiser, written evidence for each claim, your approved claim sentences, and banned phrases for this product. If a platform, network or regulator asks why you said something, you can show it. And it stops you drifting into stronger claims as you make new creatives.

takeaways: Disease claims (cure, treat, prevent) are for licensed medicines only; keep ads to true product facts and supported claims.
Softening words do not fix a misleading claim; regulators judge the overall impression.
You are responsible for the lander you send traffic to, including the network's.

lessons.title: Health claims law by region
objectives: By the end you can name the main regulators for health product ads in your target geos.
By the end you can explain the difference between the EU approved-list system and the US evidence system.
By the end you can check a product's registration and a claim's legal status before running.

steps.h: Every country writes its own rules
steps.p: There is no single global rule for health ads. Each country decides which products need registration, which claims are allowed and whether ads must be approved before they run. Fines, product seizures and criminal charges are possible in some places. You need to know the basics for every geo you run.

d.s: Check each geo before you spend

steps.say: There's no single global rule for health ads. Each country decides which products need registration, which claims are allowed, and whether ads must be approved before they run. In some places, fines, product seizures and criminal charges are possible. The law changes at the border, so you need to know the basics for every geo you run, and check each one before you spend.

steps.h: This lesson is a map, not legal advice
steps.p: We describe the main systems so you know where to look. Laws and guidance change, and how they apply to online affiliate ads is not always clear. For anything you are unsure about, check the regulator's own website or ask a local lawyer.

d.text: Not legal advice. Laws change. Check the regulator's current guidance for your product and geo, and ask a qualified local lawyer when unsure.

steps.say: Before we start, an important note. This lesson is a map, not legal advice. We describe the main systems so you know where to look. Laws and guidance change, and how they apply to online affiliate ads isn't always clear. Check the regulator's current guidance for your product and geo, and ask a qualified local lawyer when you're unsure.

steps.p: Most countries follow one of two broad ideas. Some keep a list of approved health claims and allow nothing else. Others let you make claims you can prove with good evidence. Both ban disease claims for non-medicines.

rows: Only claims on an official register
Any truthful claim backed by solid proof
Product and some ads approved first

steps.say: Most countries follow one of two broad ideas. The approved list system, used in the E U and U K, allows only claims on an official register. The evidence based system, like the U S under the F T C, allows any truthful claim backed by solid proof. And there's a third pattern, registration and ad approval, where the product and some ads are approved first, as in Nigeria, Ghana and others. Both main systems ban disease claims for non medicines.

steps.p: The FTC polices deceptive ads and expects competent and reliable scientific evidence for health claims, usually good human studies. The FDA lets supplements make structure or function claims but not disease claims. FTC guides on endorsements also apply.
steps.more: The FTC's 2022 Health Products Compliance Guidance explains the evidence it expects. A structure or function claim on a supplement label must carry the FDA disclaimer. The disclaimer does not make a false claim legal. We are not certain of every current detail; check ftc.gov and fda.gov.
d: Disclaimer|'not intended to diagnose, treat, cure or prevent any disease'
steps.say: In the United States, the F T C, Federal Trade Commission, polices deceptive ads and expects solid scientific evidence for health claims, usually good human studies. The F D A, Food and Drug Administration, lets supplements make structure or function claims, but not disease claims. Those labels carry a disclaimer: not intended to diagnose, treat, cure or prevent any disease. But the disclaimer doesn't make a false claim legal. F T C endorsement guides apply too. We're not certain of every current detail, so check the regulators' own sites.

steps.p: In the EU, health claims on foods and supplements must come from the approved list under Regulation 1924/2006. The UK keeps its own register and the ASA enforces the CAP Code. Claims to treat or prevent disease are banned for foods and supplements.
steps.more: Example: a joint supplement with vitamin C may use the listed claim 'Vitamin C contributes to normal collagen formation for the normal function of cartilage', if it contains enough vitamin C to qualify. It may not say the product helps arthritis. Many herbal claims are not on the list at all. Check the current register for exact wording and conditions.
d: Example claim|'Vitamin C contributes to the normal function of the immune system'
UK|GB register, ASA and CAP Code
Cosmetics|claims must be truthful and supported
Filters|ASA has ruled against beauty filters that exaggerate results
steps.say: In the E U, health claims on foods and supplements must come from the approved list under Regulation nineteen twenty four of two thousand and six. An example of a listed claim: Vitamin C contributes to the normal function of the immune system. The U K keeps its own register, and the A S A enforces the CAP Code. Cosmetic claims must be truthful and supported. The A S A has ruled against beauty filters that exaggerate results. And claims to treat or prevent disease are banned for foods and supplements.

steps.p: Example: searching an approved claims register for one nutrient. The pattern is the same in most registers: search the nutrient, read the exact wording and the conditions of use. Layout and names change; check the current official register.

rows: Contributes to normal collagen formation for the normal function of cartilage

blocks.value: Conditions: the food must be at least a source of vitamin C.

steps.say: Here's an example of searching an approved claims register for one nutrient, vitamin C. Look at the results. Contributes to normal collagen formation for the normal function of cartilage, authorised. Protects joints from arthritis, not authorised. And notice the condition underneath: the food must be at least a source of vitamin C. The pattern is the same in most registers: search the nutrient, read the exact wording, and read the conditions of use. Layouts change, so check the current official register.

steps.p: These are the main bodies to check. Whether a product needs registration, and whether an ad needs approval, depends on the product type. We are not certain how each rule is applied to online affiliate ads; check current guidance with the regulator.

rows: Registration and ad approval for many products

steps.say: Here's where to look in Africa. Nigeria, NAFDAC and ARCON, with product registration and ads vetted. Ghana, the Food and Drugs Authority, with registration and ad approval for many products. Kenya, the Pharmacy and Poisons Board and KEBS, depending on product type. South Africa, SAHPRA and the Advertising Regulatory Board, with complementary medicines rules. Cameroon, the Ministry of Public Health. We're not certain how each rule is applied to online affiliate ads, so check current guidance with the regulator.

steps.say: Here's an example of checking a product's registration for a Nigerian offer. Treat it as the pattern, not exact clicks. Step one, ask the network for the registration number in writing. Step two, look it up on the regulator's site or verification service. Step three, compare the details: name, maker, product type and form. In this example, the register lists it as a cosmetic, but the offer sells it as a joint cure. That's a mismatch. Step four, decide. If it isn't registered, or the category doesn't match the claims, don't run it.

steps.h: Same product, legal and illegal copy
steps.p: Example: a vitamin C and collagen supplement for an EU geo. The left column breaks the approved-list rules. The right column uses product facts and a listed claim, subject to the product meeting the conditions for that claim.

b.title: Within the rules
items: Vitamin C contributes to normal collagen formation for the normal function of cartilage
Contains 80 mg vitamin C per capsule

steps.say: Here's the same product with legal and illegal copy, a vitamin C and collagen supplement for an E U geo. On the left, breaking the rules: rebuilds damaged cartilage, ends joint pain, clinically proven miracle, better than your pills. On the right, within the rules: the listed claim about vitamin C and collagen formation for cartilage, contains eighty milligrams of vitamin C per capsule, one capsule a day, and food supplement, not a medicine. That's subject to the product meeting the conditions for that claim.

steps.h: Is the claim worth the risk?
steps.p: Example sum to keep in mind. A stronger claim might lift leads, but the expected loss from a ban, refunds and fines usually outweighs it. You cannot price legal risk precisely, which is exactly why the starting rule is: do not make the claim.
steps.more: Example: a cure claim adds $40 a day of profit for 20 days, $800. If there is even a 1 in 2 chance it gets the account disabled, and a disable costs $3,150 in lost profit, the expected loss is $1,575. $800 − $1,575 = −$775. The numbers are invented to show the shape; real fines and harm to buyers make it worse.
steps.say: Is a stronger claim worth the risk? The equation on screen: extra profit, minus the chance of a ban times its cost, equals your real gain. For example, a cure claim adds forty dollars a day for twenty days, eight hundred dollars. If there's even a one in two chance it gets the account disabled, at three thousand one hundred and fifty dollars, the expected loss is one thousand five hundred and seventy five. So the real gain is minus seven hundred and seventy five. The numbers are invented to show the shape. You can't price legal risk precisely, so the starting rule is: don't make the claim.

takeaways: The EU and UK allow only listed health claims; the US requires solid evidence; many African countries require registration and sometimes ad approval.
Verify registration yourself and check that the category matches the claims.
A disclaimer never makes a false or disease claim legal.

lessons.title: Platform health policies: Meta and TikTok
objectives: By the end you can name the main platform rules that affect health and beauty ads.
By the end you can rewrite copy that breaks the personal attributes and negative self-perception rules.
By the end you can respond to a rejected ad without harming your account.

steps.h: The platform is a second regulator
steps.p: Even where the law allows a claim, Meta and TikTok may not. Their policies on health and appearance are often stricter than the law, and they enforce them with automated review, account quality scores and bans. Your ad must pass both.
steps.say: Think of the platform as a second regulator. Even where the law allows a claim, Meta and TikTok may not. Their policies on health and appearance are often stricter than the law, and they enforce them with automated review, account quality scores and bans. Legal isn't enough. Your ad must pass both.

steps.p: Platform policies change often and differ by country. What follows is how the rules have worked at the time of writing. We are not certain this is current; check the platform's Help Center and ad policies before relying on it.

steps.p: These areas cause most nutra rejections on both platforms. Exact wording differs between Meta and TikTok and changes over time, so read the current policy pages before each campaign. Rough guide only.

rows: No shaming of body or looks
Do not imply you know the viewer's health

steps.say: These areas cause most nutra rejections on both platforms. Before and after: no side by side results images, like two belly photos. Negative self perception: no shaming of body or looks, like hate your wrinkles. Personal attributes: don't imply you know the viewer's health, like your joint pain ends now. Unrealistic results, like lose ten kilos in seven days. Unsafe substances, with some ingredients banned outright. And age, with weight loss limited to adults. Exact wording differs and changes, so this is a rough guide only.

steps.p: Meta's personal attributes rule bans copy that asserts or implies you know something personal about the viewer, including health conditions. Talk about the product or people in general, not 'you' and your condition.
steps.more: These are teaching examples, not guarantees. Review is partly automated and can still reject compliant ads or let bad ones through for a while. Write for the policy, not for the reviewer.

b.title: Passes more often
items: A cooling cream for tired knees
Made for long days on your feet
What is in our low-sugar range

steps.say: Meta's personal attributes rule bans copy that asserts or implies you know something personal about the viewer, including health conditions. On the left, copy that fails: do you have arthritis, your knees hurt every morning, other diabetics love this, still overweight? On the right, copy that passes more often: a cooling cream for tired knees, made for long days on your feet, what's in our low sugar range, a simple walking routine guide. These are teaching examples, not guarantees. Review is partly automated, so write for the policy, not for the reviewer.

steps.p: Treat a rejection as feedback, not as an obstacle to get around. Repeated rejections lower account quality, and trying to trick review breaks the rules. Starting rules; adapt to your account history.

steps.h: Policy mistakes that get accounts banned

lessons.title: Before-and-after, body image and fake experts

steps.h: The oldest tricks are the most banned
steps.p: Before-and-after photos, actors in white coats, celebrity faces and 'doctors hate this' headlines were common in nutra for years. Today they are banned by platforms, illegal in many countries and a fast route to a disabled account. They also hurt people who believe them.

d.s: No fake doctors, no fake celebrities

steps.say: Before and after photos, actors in white coats, celebrity faces, and doctors hate this headlines were common in nutra for years. Today they're banned by platforms, illegal in many countries, and a fast route to a disabled account. They also hurt people who believe them. So the rule is simple. No fake proof. No fake doctors, and no fake celebrities.

steps.p: Each of these misleads the buyer about who stands behind the product or what it will do. Platforms block them, and consumer and advertising law in most countries treats them as deception.
d: Before-and-after|implies results most buyers will not get
Body shaming|harms self-image, banned on platforms
Celebrity faces|uses a real person without consent
Fake news pages|pretends to be journalism
steps.say: Here's what's banned, and why. Before and after implies results most buyers won't get. Body shaming harms self image, and is banned on platforms. Fake doctors invent medical authority. Celebrity faces use a real person without consent. Deepfakes are A I copies of real people. And fake news pages pretend to be journalism. Each one misleads the buyer about who stands behind the product, or what it will do. Consumer and advertising law in most countries treats them as deception.

steps.p: Using a real person's face, voice or name without written permission is likely to break platform policy, consumer law and that person's rights. AI-generated copies of real doctors or celebrities are the same. Platforms are actively hunting these ads.

d.text: Never use a real person's likeness without written permission, never invent experts, and never use AI copies of real people. This school does not teach any form of fake endorsement.

steps.h: Why honest visuals can cost less per buyer
steps.p: Example: one cream, two creatives, 100 leads each. The before-and-after creative is cheaper per lead before it is rejected, but fewer buyers approve and accept the parcel because the product cannot match the picture.
steps.more: Example: payout $20 per approved lead, buyout-linked payout cut to $14 when buyout falls under the offer's line. Before-and-after: 40% approval, buyout under the line, so $14 × 0.4 = $5.60 per lead. Honest routine: 50% approval, buyout fine, $20 × 0.5 = $10 per lead. And the first creative usually gets rejected anyway.

The honest routine gets fifty percent approval at the full payout, ten dollars per lead. Look at the bars. And the first creative usually gets rejected anyway.

steps.h: How a fake endorsement spreads harm
steps.p: One fake endorsement does damage at every step. The buyer is misled, the call centre has to manage false hope, the parcel is refused, the network cuts payouts and the platform disables the account. This is why networks with real advertisers ban them too.
steps.say: This map shows how one fake endorsement spreads harm. Follow it from the fake doctor ad. A click brings a misled buyer. Their order leads to hard calls for the call centre. Doubt leads to a refused parcel. Low buyout leads to a payout cut from the network. And on the other branch, platform review leads to a disabled account. Damage at every step. That's why networks with real advertisers ban fake endorsements too.

lessons.title: Honest testimonials and disclaimers
objectives: By the end you can collect real customer testimonials with consent and proper disclosure.
By the end you can explain why 'results not typical' does not fix a misleading testimonial.
By the end you can place a disclaimer where it actually informs the buyer.

steps.h: Real people, real words, real disclosure
steps.p: Testimonials are powerful because people trust other buyers. That is why fake ones are illegal in many countries and banned by platforms. A testimonial must come from a real customer, say what they actually experienced and show any payment or free product.

d.b: If it is not real, it is not a testimonial

steps.say: Testimonials are powerful because people trust other buyers. That's exactly why fake ones are illegal in many countries and banned by platforms. A testimonial must come from a real customer, say what they actually experienced, and show any payment or free product. If it isn't real, it isn't a testimonial, and it can be illegal.

steps.p: In the US, FTC endorsement guides and a 2024 rule on reviews ban fake and AI-invented reviews. The UK banned fake reviews under a 2024 law. Other countries have similar consumer rules. We are not certain of every current detail; check your geo.
d: Real buyer|who actually used the product
Real experience|their words, not your script
Typical results|or say clearly what most people get
No AI fakes|no invented people or reviews
steps.say: Here are the rules in plain words. In the U S, F T C endorsement guides and a twenty twenty four rule on reviews ban fake and A I invented reviews. The U K banned fake reviews under a twenty twenty four law, and other countries have similar consumer rules. So: a real buyer who actually used the product. Their real experience, in their words, not your script. Typical results, or say clearly what most people get. Disclose free product, payment or relationship. Written consent. And no A I fakes. We're not certain of every detail, so check your geo.

steps.p: Each of these can turn a useful testimonial into a deceptive ad, and some are illegal on their own. The fixes are simple and usually cost nothing more than honesty and a little patience.
steps.more: A testimonial is still your claim. If a customer says 'it cured my arthritis', you cannot use that line even if they believe it, because the ad would make a disease claim. Pick parts of what they said that are true and allowed, without changing the meaning.

a.title: Mistakes
items: Scripting cure claims for a customer
Hiding that the product was free
Showing the best result as normal

b.title: Fixes
items: Customers say only what is true and allowed

steps.say: Each of these mistakes can turn a useful testimonial into a deceptive ad. On the left: writing reviews yourself, scripting cure claims for a customer, hiding that the product was free, and showing the best result as normal. On the right: only real customer words, customers say only what's true and allowed, disclose it on screen, and show typical experiences. And remember, a testimonial is still your claim. If a customer says it cured my arthritis, you can't use that line, even if they believe it.

steps.h: Asking a customer for a testimonial
steps.p: Example message to a real buyer, sent by the advertiser or with the network's permission. It asks for honest words, offers a disclosed thank-you that does not depend on a positive review and asks for consent.

messages.text: Hello Ada, thank you for your order. Would you share an honest short video about using the cream? Good or bad is fine.
We will send a free tube as thanks either way, and we will say so in the ad.
OK. Can I just say how it feels and how I use it?
Yes, exactly that. Please do not mention any illness. I will send a consent form.

steps.say: Here's an example of asking a real buyer for a testimonial, sent by the advertiser or with the network's permission. The team asks Ada for an honest short video, and says good or bad is fine. They'll send a free tube as thanks either way, and say so in the ad. Ada asks if she can just say how it feels and how she uses it. Yes, exactly that, and please don't mention any illness. Then they send a consent form. Notice the thank you doesn't depend on a positive review.

steps.p: Example: real testimonials are not free, but they are cheap compared with the risk of fakes. Budget for products, shipping and a small fee, and expect that only some videos will be usable.
steps.more: Example only. 20 × $8 = $160. If 6 videos are usable, $160 ÷ 6 = $26.67 each. Add any fees you pay creators. One good testimonial can run for weeks across many ad sets, so this is a small cost per day of use.
steps.say: Real testimonials aren't free, but they're cheap compared with the risk of fakes. In this example, twenty buyers times eight dollars of product and shipping is one hundred and sixty dollars. If six videos are usable, that's about twenty six dollars sixty seven each, plus any creator fees. Expect only some videos to be usable. And one good testimonial can run for weeks across many ad sets, so it's a small cost per day of use.

steps.h: Disclaimers do not fix false claims
steps.p: 'Results not typical' or 'individual results vary' does not make a misleading testimonial legal. If most buyers would not get the result shown, do not show it, or say clearly what most buyers can expect.

d.text: A disclaimer cannot cure a false or misleading message. Fix the message first; use disclaimers only to add true information.

steps.say: A key warning. Results not typical, or individual results vary, does not make a misleading testimonial legal. If most buyers wouldn't get the result shown, don't show it, or say clearly what most buyers can expect. A disclaimer can't cure a false or misleading message. Fix the message first, and use disclaimers only to add true information.

steps.p: A disclaimer must be seen and understood by the buyer, in their language, close to the claim it qualifies. Hidden footers and tiny grey text do not count with most regulators.

rows: On screen while the claim shows, long enough to read
Next to the claim, readable size
Near the claim and before the form
English only in a French geo

In a video, on screen while the claim shows, long enough to read, not one frame at the end. In an image, next to the claim at a readable size, not tiny corner text. On a lander, near the claim and before the form, not only in the footer. And in the buyer's language, not English only in a French geo.

A counter that never changes is deceptive. Real reviews, all shown, is honest. And no rating at all is honest and fine. Only show ratings from a real, checkable review system, and only the real figure.

takeaways: Testimonials must come from real buyers, in their own words, with consent and disclosed incentives.
A testimonial is still your claim; no disease or cure statements even if the buyer said them.
Disclaimers must be clear and close to the claim, and never fix a misleading message.

objectives: By the end you can run a full compliance review of an offer, creative, lander and call script before launch.
By the end you can apply starting rules for rejections, warnings and pushy network requests.
By the end you can keep records that protect you if questions come later.

steps.p: Compliance works when it is a habit, not a panic. A short, fixed review before every launch catches most problems before a platform or regulator does. It costs minutes. Skipping it can cost the account, the payout and harm to buyers.

d.s: Every offer, every creative, every lander

steps.say: Compliance works when it's a habit, not a panic. A short, fixed review before every launch catches most problems before a platform or regulator does. It costs minutes. Skipping it can cost the account, the payout, and harm to buyers. So review before you spend. Every offer, every creative, every lander.

steps.p: Your responsibility covers the whole path a buyer takes, not just the ad. The ad, the lander, the order form, the call centre script and even the parcel insert can contain claims. Ask the network for the call script and the insert text.
steps.say: Your responsibility covers the whole path a buyer takes, not just the ad. Follow the map. The product and its registration feed the claims in the ad copy and video. A click leads to the lander, then the order form and consent, then the lead goes to the call script, and everything is logged in your claims file. The ad, the lander, the form, the call centre script, and even the parcel insert can contain claims. So ask the network for the call script and the insert text.

steps.p: Do these steps in order before every launch, including small creative refreshes. If any step fails, stop, fix the problem and start the review again from that step. Tap through each one.

steps.title: Product
steps.text: Registration checked, category matches claims, ingredients listed.

steps.title: Ad
steps.text: Every sentence is on the approved list. No personal attributes, no before-and-after, no fake people.

steps.title: Call script
steps.text: Ask the network for the script. Operators must not make claims your ad avoids.

steps.title: Log and launch
steps.text: Save screenshots and the date. Then launch.

steps.say: Here's the pre launch review. Do the steps in order before every launch, including small creative refreshes. Step one, product: registration checked, category matches claims, ingredients listed. Step two, ad: every sentence on the approved list, no personal attributes, no before and after, no fake people. Step three, lander and form: the same claims as the ad, a disclaimer near claims, a privacy notice and consent on the form. Step four, call script: operators must not make claims your ad avoids. Step five, save screenshots and the date, then launch. If any step fails, stop, fix it, and restart from that step.

steps.h: The call centre is part of your funnel
steps.p: If an operator promises a cure on the phone, the buyer hears a cure claim that started with your ad. Ask to see the call script, and raise it with the network if it makes claims you would never put in an ad.

steps.say: These are starting rules for the moments when money pushes you towards a shortcut. Ad rejected once, fix the cause and make a new ad. Two or more rejections under the same policy in twenty four hours, stop launching and audit everything. Account warning, pause launches, fix, and appeal only if compliant. Network sends a non compliant lander, use your own honest lander. Network insists on banned claims, leave the offer. Product not registered where required, don't run. Write them in your plan, adapt them as you learn, but never loosen the bottom two.

steps.h: Saying no to a pushy manager
steps.p: Network managers are paid on volume, and some push affiliates to use aggressive creatives. A polite, firm reply in writing protects you and often gets a better answer than you expect.

quiz.q: Which items belong in a pre-launch review?
options: Product, ad, lander, form, call script and insert
quiz.why: Claims can appear anywhere on the buyer's path.

quiz.q: The call script promises to 'cure joint pain'. What do you do?
options: Ignore it, it is not your ad
Ask the network to change it or do not run the offer
quiz.why: The call is part of your funnel; a cure claim there is a real problem.

quiz.q: The manager insists you use a fake doctor video. Starting rule?
options: Use it in one ad set
Refuse, and leave the offer if they insist
Ask for a higher payout first
quiz.why: Fake experts are banned and deceptive. Leave the offer if it requires them.

lessons.say_intro: In this final lesson you'll put everything together into a pre launch compliance workflow. You'll review the whole path a buyer takes, apply clear decision rules, and keep records that protect you later.
lessons.say_outro: So, review before you spend, check the whole path from product to call script, decide your rules before the pressure arrives, say no in writing, and keep dated records. Your task: build a one page pre launch checklist from this lesson and use it on one offer today, including asking the network for its call script. Now take the quiz.

exam.q: Your ad says 'May help reverse diabetes'. What is the problem?
options: It is a disease claim; softening words do not fix it
exam.why: Reversing a disease is a medical claim. Regulators judge the overall impression.

exam.q: An EU supplement offer. Which claim approach is right?
options: Only claims from the approved register, with their conditions
exam.why: The EU allows only authorised health claims for foods and supplements.

exam.q: Two ads are rejected for 'personal health' within a day. What next?
options: Launch the same ads in a new campaign
Stop launching and audit all live ads and the lander
Raise budget on the remaining ads
exam.why: A pattern of rejections means something systematic; audit before launching more.

exam.q: A creative shows a split-screen belly photo. Decision?
options: Do not run; before-and-after is banned and misleading
exam.why: Before-and-after images are banned for health and appearance products on major platforms.

exam.q: Example: a claim adds $600 profit, with a 50% chance of a $2,000 loss. Expected result?
A customer video says 'this cream healed my arthritis'. How do you use it?
options: As is, it is their opinion
Use only true, allowed parts without changing meaning, or not at all
Add a doctor next to it
exam.why: A testimonial becomes your claim; disease claims stay out.

exam.q: The product is registered as a cosmetic, the offer sells it for joint disease. What do you do?
options: Run cosmetic claims only with your own lander, or skip
exam.why: The registered category limits the claims you can make.

exam.q: A creator received free product and a fee. What must the ad show?
options: A clear disclosure of the free product and payment
exam.why: Material connections must be clearly disclosed.

exam.q: Meta's Events Manager limits health events for your account. What do you do?
options: Follow the limits and check the Help Center for current options
exam.why: Renaming or hiding data to get around restrictions is circumvention.

exam.q: Weight management offer, policy requires 18+. Audience 4.0 million, 2.6 million at 18+. What share is left, and what age do you set?
